food.text: The Capsian people of Algeria and Tunisia, active from about 9000 to 5400 cal BC, ate a wide variety of animals. Their diet ranged from aurochs and hartebeest to hares and snails. There is little evidence about which plants they ate.

Around the salt lakes of Tunisia, food gatherers built up shell middens. They were later succeeded by simple food producers, with little change in their flint industry. This later phase has been described as a 'Neolithic of Capsian tradition'.

A Neolithic society marked by domestication and subsistence agriculture developed in the Maghreb and Sahara between 6000 and 2000 BC. It is richly depicted in the paintings of the Tassili n'Ajjer region of southeastern Algeria.

In the Capsian period the Maghreb was open savanna, much like modern East Africa, with Mediterranean forests at higher altitudes. Its early phase overlapped with the African humid period. This was the landscape in which Capsian people lived and found their food.

In Tunisia, native food gatherers were apparently not displaced by immigrant farmers from the east. They adopted a food-producing economy themselves, in what has been described as a 'Neolithic of Capsian tradition'.
In the Maghreb, a simple farming culture survived very little altered for millennia. Because of this, a site with impressed pottery might date to the sixth millennium BC or to the second.

art.text: The Capsian was an Epipalaeolithic tradition in Algeria and Tunisia from about 9000 to 5400 cal BC. Its sites hold decorative art, including both figurative and abstract rock art.
Cave paintings found in the Tassili n'Ajjer region of southeastern Algeria have been dated to twelve millennia before present. Other rock art has been found at Tadrart Acacus in the Libyan desert.
The Tassili n'Ajjer cave paintings, north of Tamanrasset in Algeria, show vibrant and vivid scenes of everyday life. They date to the Neolithic Subpluvial period, about 8000 to 4000 BCE.
Capsian people made ornaments and containers from natural materials. Ostrich eggshells were turned into beads and containers, while seashells were used for necklaces.
Ochre has been found at Capsian sites on both tools and corpses. This use of colored pigment sits alongside the tradition's rock art and shell ornaments.

Capsian settlements are known from escargotières, mounds of ash, stone tools, animal bones and land snail shells. The same civilization left evidence of rock art, sculpting, polishing and pottery, with notable mounds at Medjez Amar and Mechta Sidi El Arbi near Constantine.

In Numidia, older unpainted pottery was decorated with incisions, grooves, projections and other relief or recessed patterns. Some of its forms date back to the Neolithic period, showing how long these craft traditions lasted in the Maghreb.

science.text: Some 9,000 years ago, Earth's tilt was 24.14 degrees, compared with 23.45 degrees today. Around 3,500 BC, changes in the tilt of Earth's orbit appear to have caused rapid desertification of the Sahara. The new desert became a natural barrier that severely limited contact between the Maghreb and sub-Saharan Africa.

Some parts of North Africa began to take part in the Neolithic revolution in the 6th millennium BCE, just before the rapid desertification of the Sahara around 3500 BC. Domesticated plants and animals were introduced during this period, spreading from the north and east to the southwest.

The end of the last glacial period brought more rain to the Sahara, from about 8000 BC to 6000 BC, perhaps because of low pressure areas over the collapsing ice sheets to the north. By around 4200 BC, the monsoon had retreated south to roughly where it is today, leading to the gradual desertification of the Sahara.

In prehistoric times, the Sahara to the south and the Mediterranean Sea to the north were important barriers to newcomers from Sub-Saharan Africa and Europe. Northwest Africa also went through long periods of genetic isolation, which allowed distinctive genetic markers to evolve, especially in certain isolated Berber-speaking groups.
A Neolithic society marked by domestication and subsistence agriculture developed in the Maghreb from about 6000 BC. Its way of life is richly depicted in the Tassili n'Ajjer paintings.

Researchers have inferred a connection between areas of rapid drying and the introduction of livestock in North Africa. The natural, orbital aridification was amplified by the spread of shrubs and open land caused by grazing.

Around 5000 BC, the populations of North Africa were primarily descended from the makers of the Iberomaurusian and Capsian cultures. A more recent intrusion was associated with the Neolithic Revolution.

The Afroasiatic language family, to which the Berber languages belong, probably originated during the Mesolithic period. This may have happened in the context of the Capsian culture, according to the source.

A 2025 Harvard University study analyzed DNA from nine late Stone Age individuals from Tunisia and Algeria. One sample from Djebba, Tunisia, showed European hunter-gatherer ancestry dating to around 8,000 BP, likely due to human migrations across the Sicilian Straits.

DNA analysis has found commonalities between Berber Moroccan populations and the Sami people of Scandinavia. The shared link dates from around 9,000 years ago, a surprising connection across a great distance.

West Asia and North Africa form a single land mass at the Sinai. Neolithic West Asian populations would have been attracted to a wet Sahara, arriving through the Suez, the Bab el-Mandeb or the Mediterranean.

culture.text: The Capsian was an Epipalaeolithic tradition in Algeria and Tunisia that lasted from about 9000 to 5400 cal BC. It is named after the town of Gafsa, Tunisia, which was called Capsa in Latin.

The Maghreb is believed to have been inhabited by Berbers from at least 10,000 BC. Cave paintings dated to twelve millennia before present have been found in the Tassili n'Ajjer region of southeastern Algeria. Other rock art was discovered at Tadrart Acacus in the Libyan desert.

Capsian sites hold decorative art, including both figurative and abstract rock art. Ochre is found on both tools and corpses. Ostrich eggshells were used to make beads and containers, and seashells were used for necklaces. The Iberomaurusian practice of extracting the central incisors, pulling the front teeth, continued sporadically but became rarer.

Capsian people lived in a Maghreb of open savanna, much like modern East Africa, with Mediterranean forests at higher altitudes. Their diet included a wide variety of animals, from aurochs and hartebeest to hares and snails.

Megalithic tombs, also called dolmens, were built as burial sites for ancient Berbers, and the article describes them as huge tombs underground, in several shapes. They date to the period before the invention of early writing in 3,200 BC. Archaeological research on prehistoric tombs in the Maghreb shows the bodies of the dead were painted with ochre and usually buried in a fetal position. Some were also buried with ostrich eggshells, jewellery and weapons.

Human remains from the earliest Neolithic contexts in northwestern Africa, dated to around 5400 BC, show European Neolithic ancestry. This suggests the first stages of farming there began with the migration of Neolithic farmers from Iberia, and the earliest pottery in the Tingitan peninsula was of Cardial type.

In a bazina, the access to the burial chamber is invisible. The deceased is buried on the ground and covered by a projecting funerary structure. Bazinas are found near Chellala and Tamda in Algeria, and in the Meknes region of Morocco at the Gour bazina.

Food gatherers built up shell middens around the salt lakes of Tunisia. They were succeeded by simple food producers with little change in their flint industry, described as a Neolithic of Capsian tradition. Native food gatherers were not displaced by immigrant farmers but adopted a food-producing economy themselves.
